newsitem.title: UK: UK's Labour unclear on BA /American deal.
newsitem.headline: UK's Labour unclear on BA /American deal.

text.p: It is far from clear whether a new government in Britain would place fresh regulatory obstacles in the way of British Airways Plc and its proposed alliance with American Airlines.

Weeks of waiting for incumbent Trade Minister Ian Lang to agree conditions with the two airlines for clearing the deal has prompted recent media speculation that the deal will not get the go-ahead before the British election.

The opposition Labour Party, seen by pollsters as the clear favourite to win the election, criticised the deal last year, calling for a lengthy investigation by Britain's Monopolies and Mergers Commission(MMC).
But Labour is no longer so certain.

"This decision has important implications for competition and the interest of consumers and British carriers and it can only responsibly be made when we are in possession of the full facts," shadow Transport Minister Andrew Smith said in a statement dictated to Reuters by his office.

"Before taking a decision on an MMC decision in these circumstances we would need to have access to all the relevant information and to evaluate the implications for consumers and all British carriers of the conditions proposed, including the state of negotiations on the proposed air services agreement (with the U.S)," he said.

The BA and American tie-up has attracted widespread criticism from rival airlines and consumer groups, alleging that the deal would monopolise transatlantic air services out of London's Heathrow airport.
But party sources said Labour would not automatically refer the deal to the MMC should it come to power before the current Government has ruled on the deal.

Instead, Labour was likely to take a pragmatic approach, they said, treating the competition issues in the context of current open skies talks between Britain and the U.S. aimed at liberalising their aviation market.
"We will obviously see what progress has been made because it (the proposed alliance) is obviously involved in the open skies negotiations," a party official said.

"We will see where it has got to and see what proposals are on the table with the overriding objective of promoting fair competition, the success of all British carriers and safeguarding British consumer interests," the official added.
Under the proposed alliance BA intends to co-ordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

BA and American argue that their deal will lead to greater competition because an open skies deal would allow all U.S. airlines access to compete at London Heathrow, Europe's most important transatlantic landfall.

Under the current bilateral aviation treaty only four airlines are allowed to operate services out of Heathrow -- BA, Virgin Atlantic, United Airlines and American -- and frequencies and routes are restricted.
The United States has made approval of the alliance conditional on getting an open skies deal.

But conversely Britain has made an open skies deal conditional on getting U.S. approval of the alliance, arguing that such alliances are the only way to compete for transatlantic transfer traffic in the huge U.S. domestic market, where foreign airlines are banned.

Lang proposed in December his government's conditions for allowing the alliance through, with a core demand that BA release 168 weekly runway slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights -- to make room for competitors.

But other airlines have said in formal responses to the proposals that more concessions needed to be made if BA and American were to be prevented from dominating the market, with 62 percent of current capacity.
Airline sources say the open skies talks cannot now advance until Lang gives a final ruling, since slots at Heathrow is such a key issue.

BA denied it had any fears that the British election could interrupt the approvals process. "We have no concerns," said a spokesman. "We are confident the alliance will get all the approvals required...Timings are not the issue -- the approvals are."
